articles.title: HELOC Balances Post Their Largest Quarterly Rise Since 2005
articles.description: New York Fed data show a $23 billion HELOC increase, while a reporting gap explains part of the quarter’s larger mortgage gain.
articles.summary: Home equity borrowing expanded again in the third quarter. Credit union lenders should separate that signal from a mortgage reporting correction and from mixed delinquency trends.
articles.bodyHtml:
Home equity line of credit balances rose by $23 billion in the third quarter of 2026, reaching $481 billion, according to the New York Fed’s November 10 household debt release. It was the largest quarterly increase since 2005. HELOC credit limits also expanded, by $31 billion.

For credit union lending teams building next year’s production plans, those figures provide a reason to examine demand for home equity credit. They do not establish how much of the growth came from credit unions, which borrowers drew on existing lines, or how the money was spent.

The most eye-catching housing number requires particular care. Mortgage balances increased by $257 billion, but the full quarterly report says roughly half of that increase reflected balances returning to the data after a reporting gap in the previous quarter. Treating the entire increase as new borrowing would overstate the change in household behavior.

Growth and credit quality tell different stories

The report marks an eighteenth consecutive quarterly increase in HELOC balances. Across all household borrowing, however, the share of debt in some stage of delinquency reached 5.0%, up from 4.7% in the previous quarter. Those totals combine products with different performance patterns.

The New York Fed’s reported flow of balances into serious delinquency was 1.17% for HELOCs, compared with 1.27% a year earlier. The comparable mortgage figure increased from 1.28% to 1.60%. These measures track balances becoming at least 90 days late; they are not the percentage of all balances already in serious delinquency. The release describes HELOC serious-delinquency transitions as flat from the preceding quarter.

That combination matters for portfolio interpretation. Rising outstanding balances and a relatively stable transition rate can coexist. Neither measure, taken alone, tells a lender whether a new group of borrowers is performing better or whether an existing group is using more of its available credit.

A national benchmark needs a local explanation

A useful internal comparison would separate new lines, increased limits and additional draws on existing accounts. A credit union whose balances are growing mainly through repeat draws faces a different planning question from one adding new borrowers. The first needs to understand utilization and repayment capacity; the second needs to understand acquisition costs and the performance of recent originations.

These are analytical questions prompted by the release, rather than findings about credit unions. The public report draws on anonymized Equifax credit records across lenders. It does not identify a credit union segment or provide a ready-made forecast for an individual institution.

The New York Fed’s methodology notes add two useful cautions for finance and risk presentations. Balances are nominal, without an inflation adjustment. The credit-score charts also switched to VantageScore 4.0 in the first quarter of 2026, so comparisons across that boundary can reflect a model change as well as a change in borrowers.

For a lending committee, the strongest use of this release is a product-level comparison with the credit union’s own experience. The HELOC expansion is a clear national development. Its effect on local opportunity, concentration and repayment risk still needs to be established from member-level portfolio data.

articles.title: FedNow’s 2027 Credits Come With Volume Tests and a Fee Cap
articles.description: The 2027 FedNow incentives can reduce implementation costs, but credit unions need to model eligibility, continuing service costs and reversal risk.
articles.summary: A FedNow incentive is worth the amount a credit union can qualify for and retain. The program’s fee cap, sender thresholds and service requirements belong in the business case before a headline discount does.
articles.bodyHtml:
Credit unions evaluating FedNow for 2027 have a new financial incentive to consider. Federal Reserve Financial Services will offer statement credits for qualifying send and receive capabilities beginning January 1. The program announcement, published September 15, also says the existing origination discount on the first 2,500 monthly items will end.

The business case therefore needs a fresh comparison. An institution may receive a credit while losing an existing discount, adding supporting services and incurring implementation costs. The practical question for a CFO is how much of the incentive the credit union can retain after meeting its obligations.

Start with the eligible amount

The 2027 fee schedule lists the following maximum credits. The actual statement credit cannot exceed the customer’s total fees paid in the preceding 12 months. Both new and existing FedNow participants can qualify.

Institution’s FedACH statusReceive maximumSend maximum
FedNow enabled; no higher FedACH tier$5,000$20,000
Eligible for FedACH Receipt Discount Program$10,000$40,000
Participating in FedACH Receipt Discount Program$20,000$80,000

That distinction between eligibility and participation is consequential. A credit union should establish its applicable tier and the effect of the fee cap with its FRFS relationship manager before treating a maximum amount as a budget assumption. The schedule alone does not establish a particular institution’s entitlement.

FRFS has also published the continuing transaction prices: 4.5 cents for a customer credit transfer origination, with the general $25 monthly participation fee per routing number discounted to zero in 2027. These prices help identify the Federal Reserve component of operating cost. They do not supply a processor’s charges, integration expense, staffing needs or fraud losses.

The sender credit has a performance condition

Under the program terms, the basic send tier requires at least 100 transactions a month. The higher tiers require at least 2,500. Existing senders already at the applicable threshold must increase average monthly send volume by at least 50% over the prior-year baseline.

Institutions must opt in. Half the credit is applied then and half after qualification. The volume test must be met in six qualifying months within the calendar year or six months after opt-in, whichever period is longer; the months need not be consecutive. Completed customer credit transfer originations count. Failure to meet the test can reverse the initial credit.

Consider an illustrative credit union qualifying for the full $20,000 basic send incentive after application of the fee cap. The payment sequence would be $10,000 at opt-in and $10,000 after qualification. If adoption falls short, the first $10,000 may have to be reversed. That makes a forecast of actual completed payments more useful than a forecast of registrations or enrolled accounts.

For internal planning, show the project with the full eligible incentive and again with no retained incentive. This is an economic sensitivity analysis, not a recommendation about accounting recognition. It makes the dependence on payment adoption visible to the committee approving the investment.

Receiving also carries continuing obligations

The receive credit requires full participation in the Exception Resolution Service, a FedPayments Insights subscription, and either FedDetect Anomaly Notification Premier or an integrated pre-transaction fraud service. Required services must remain active for six months. A failure to maintain them can reverse the credit.

Those services may be useful in their own right. Finance and payments leaders should still establish the incremental cost of the chosen combination and whether it fits existing fraud and reconciliation work. A service already in use has a different economic effect from one purchased solely to qualify.

The result should be a costed operating decision: an eligible credit amount, a realistic usage forecast, the expenses that continue after the credit, and an owner for monitoring qualification. FRFS’s program can improve the economics of sending or receiving instant payments. A credible credit union business case shows how the service will remain useful once the incentive has been earned.

articles.title: NCUA’s First Two 2026 Charters Start With Distinct Member Groups
articles.description: Accion Opportunity plans a business-lending focus, while All Peoples United will serve associations supporting African diaspora communities.
articles.summary: The two federal charters announced October 30 show different approaches to a specific membership. Their first-year plans are concrete, while actual growth and financial performance remain unreported.
articles.bodyHtml:
The National Credit Union Administration’s first two federal charters of 2026 begin with different propositions: a credit union organized for member business lending, and one built around associations serving Cameroonian and broader African diaspora communities.

The agency announced both on October 30. Accion Opportunity Federal Credit Union, in Commerce, California, received a charter effective October 5. All Peoples United Federal Credit Union, in Columbia, Maryland, followed on October 6. Both received Share Insurance Fund coverage.

For boards considering where future membership will come from, the announcements offer a narrow but useful comparison of institutional design. They describe intended members and opening product plans. They do not yet show whether either institution has converted those relationships into sustained deposits, loan demand or operating income.

A business-lending purpose and an association base

Accion Opportunity is a multiple common bond credit union with a potential membership of about 70,000 people. It will serve members of the Accion Opportunity Member Alliance and employees of Accion Opportunity Fund Community Development. NCUA says it was chartered for the purpose of making member business loans.

Its planned first-year products connect business credit with deposit relationships: consumer and business savings and checking, personal loans, equipment financing, and secured and unsecured business loans. The intended customers include low-income individuals and small-business owners.

All Peoples United is also a multiple common bond credit union. Its principal groups are First Trust Team Corporation in Columbia and Community Solidarity Network in Upper Marlboro, Maryland. NCUA describes both organizations as supporting Cameroonian and broader African diaspora communities.

Its initial product list centers on savings and checking accounts, signature loans and auto loans. The agency’s announcement does not specify a potential membership count.

The strategic question is conversion

The useful distinction is the relationship each institution expects to build. Accion’s stated design places a business owner’s financing and transaction needs within one membership. All Peoples United’s design begins with shared association ties and an initial range of household banking products. That comparison is an interpretation of the published plans, rather than a statement about either institution’s results.

An existing credit union assessing a similar opportunity can use the same level of specificity. A named partner or an eligible population is a starting point. The next question is which financial need would cause someone to open an account, keep a balance, or use credit there. Those decisions need evidence beyond the size of the group a credit union is allowed to serve.

The 70,000 figure is particularly easy to misuse. It describes Accion’s potential membership, not enrolled members or active accounts. The source does not establish a conversion rate. Applying that number directly to a revenue forecast would therefore add an assumption that the charter announcement cannot support.

Neither release gives an opening balance sheet, capital commitment, loan production target, pricing schedule or operating break-even forecast. Those omissions limit any claim that the two charters demonstrate a proven growth model. They also define the evidence that will make the next reporting milestone more informative.

For now, the board-level lesson is specific: a membership strategy can start with an identifiable group and a limited product promise. Whether that promise produces a viable credit union will become clearer through actual account activity, funding and loan performance.

articles.title: Preparing Credit Union IRAs for the 2027 Saver’s Match
articles.description: The new retirement incentive has two separate questions: whether a member’s contribution qualifies and how the federal match reaches an account.
articles.summary: Saver’s Match applies to eligible 2027 retirement contributions, with claims filed in 2028. Credit unions can prepare clear member explanations now while tracking the still-developing payment and provider-registration process.
articles.bodyHtml:
The federal Saver’s Match begins with eligible retirement contributions for 2027, creating a new conversation for credit unions that offer IRAs. The IRS’s current explanation says an eligible saver can receive a government contribution of up to $1,000 a year, calculated at up to 50% of qualifying savings. Claims for 2027 will be made with the 2027 tax return filed in 2028.

For member-service and IRA operations teams, the important distinction is between a contribution that helps a member qualify and an account prepared to receive the federal payment. Opening an IRA, explaining eligibility and processing a government match are connected activities, but each needs its own accurate answer.

That distinction should shape preparations before campaigns promise members an automatic deposit. The program’s statutory benefit is established. Some of the machinery for delivering it remains under development.

Explain the calendar and the limits

The IRS says the Saver’s Match will replace the Saver’s Credit for eligible retirement contributions. A member may qualify even with little or no federal income tax liability. Age, student status, dependency, tax residency and income conditions also apply, so the advertised maximum is not an entitlement for every IRA holder.

The Treasury and IRS September 28 report to Congress sets out the 2027 income ranges:

Filing statusMatch begins to phase down above MAGINo match at MAGI of
Single or married filing separately$20,500$35,500
Head of household$30,750$53,250
Married filing jointly or qualifying surviving spouse$41,000$71,000

MAGI means modified adjusted gross income. It is not interchangeable with the amount of payroll deposited into a credit union account. Staff can explain the published ranges and point members to IRS eligibility information without inferring qualification from an account balance or a deposit history.

The calendar is equally important. A 2027 contribution can support a claim made in the following filing season. That interval should appear wherever the match is described, so a member making a monthly contribution does not expect a simultaneous government top-up.

Roth eligibility and payment routing are different

The congressional report explains that qualifying savings can include traditional or Roth IRA contributions. Direct federal match payments, however, generally go to an eligible non-Roth retirement vehicle. A match below $100 has a separate option to be taken as a refundable tax credit.

Notice 2026-48 describes a possible route to a Roth IRA: Treasury would first establish a conduit traditional IRA and immediately transfer the money to the chosen Roth IRA. That transfer would be a taxable Roth conversion. This is an anticipated implementation method in a notice of intent to propose regulations, rather than a completed operating process.

The notice also considers registration for traditional IRA providers and an identifying number to direct payment. It says further information will follow. Credit unions should therefore distinguish the ability to accept ordinary member contributions from verified readiness to receive a direct Saver’s Match payment.

That is a practical product question. A credit union’s IRA provider should be able to describe what it is preparing, what depends on further federal instructions and how changes will reach frontline staff. A marketing launch date does not answer those questions.

Prepare the member handoff

A useful readiness discussion starts with the points at which a member could misunderstand the offer. Someone may save in a Roth account, qualify for some match and still need additional steps to direct the payment. Another member may qualify for less than the maximum. A third may make a contribution but need help identifying the correct tax year and claim process.

Those situations call for a short, consistent explanation across branches, contact centers and digital channels. It should identify the contribution year, explain that the member must claim the benefit, and distinguish the credit union’s confirmed capabilities from federal processes still being developed. Detailed tax questions belong with the IRS guidance or the member’s tax adviser.

There is also a service issue after enrollment. If a member asks where a missing match went, staff will need a route to the team responsible for IRA payment information. That handoff can be designed before the final technical specifications arrive, without pretending those specifications are already settled.

The immediate opportunity is to make retirement saving easier to understand. The operational commitment should be equally clear: explain what the member can do, confirm what the credit union can process, and update both when Treasury and the IRS finalize the payment instructions.

articles.title: What the Proposed Vendor-Risk Guidance Would Change for Credit Unions
articles.description: The interagency proposal favors proportional vendor reviews and informed acceptance of residual risk, while leaving consumer-compliance questions unresolved.
articles.summary: NCUA and the banking agencies want oversight to reflect the risk of each vendor relationship. The useful question is how to justify that judgment when a credit union lacks complete information or bargaining power.
articles.bodyHtml:
Credit unions have until November 16 to comment on a proposal that would put more emphasis on the risk of an individual vendor relationship and on the judgment used to accept what remains unresolved. NCUA’s deadline notice confirms that the proposed guidance is nonbinding and applies to the work banks and credit unions do with third parties.

The practical issue is familiar: a small institution may depend heavily on a provider while having little ability to negotiate its contract or obtain every requested document. The proposal addresses that imbalance directly. It also raises a difficult question about when flexibility improves oversight and when it leaves important risks insufficiently examined.

This remains a proposal. The agencies announced it on September 11, and the Federal Register published it on September 15. The approaching comment deadline should not be confused with an implementation date.

Proportionality would become the organizing principle

The OCC’s summary describes an approach based on the magnitude and likelihood of harm, adjusted for an institution’s size, complexity and risk profile. Its stated aim is to avoid processes that treat every vendor as inherently high risk. The guidance would not itself create enforceable standards.

The proposed text expressly includes insured credit unions. It separates risk identification, proportionate oversight, residual-risk acceptance and governance. It recognizes that an institution may lack the bargaining power to obtain preferred contract provisions, extensive due diligence or detailed monitoring.

For a vendor manager, the resulting decision is more demanding than simply shortening a questionnaire. Suppose two providers give incomplete answers about recovery arrangements. One supports a limited administrative task; the other is essential to member access. A useful assessment would explain the different consequences of failure and the alternatives available, rather than count missing answers as though the relationships were equivalent.

That example is an analytical application of the proposal, not an agency-approved classification. Its value is in making the judgment reviewable. A board or risk committee needs to understand the exposure it is accepting, even when the available information is imperfect.

Residual risk still needs an owner

The draft says agencies do not expect elimination of all third-party risk. It allows for reasonable acceptance where further mitigation is impractical, disproportionate or constrained by limited alternatives. It also preserves the institution’s responsibility for safe and sound operations and compliance with applicable law.

This creates a useful distinction between a known limitation and an overlooked one. A team might accept a standard contract after assessing the consequences of a provider outage and the institution’s available response. That is a different decision from renewing because no one has evaluated the dependency.

A practical management record would state the missing information, the consequence that matters, who accepted the remaining exposure and what development would cause reconsideration. Those elements are this publication’s suggested way to make a decision visible; they are not a new regulatory form or a prescriptive requirement in the proposal.

The distinction also matters for internal reporting. A document-completion percentage can describe progress through a review. It cannot, by itself, show whether the credit union could continue serving members after a major provider failure. An assessment earns its place in a board packet by connecting the vendor relationship to that operating consequence.

The consumer-compliance question remains contested

The proposed text says additional consumer-compliance considerations are not directly addressed. Federal Reserve Governor Michael Barr’s dissent argues that the proposals could leave supervisory gaps or create confusion if existing guidance is rescinded. He also questions whether emphasis on material financial risk could delay correction of problems. Those are his stated objections, rather than demonstrated effects of a final policy.

The agencies’ joint announcement also distinguishes this interagency proposal from a separate proposed guide for Federal Reserve-supervised traditional community banks. The latter should not be treated as a credit union instruction merely because it was released alongside NCUA’s joint proposal.

For a credit union considering a comment, a concrete example may be more useful than general support for less paperwork. Explain which information a provider will not supply, how that limits an actual risk decision and what clarification would help. The eventual guidance will be more useful if it makes reasonable judgment easier to defend while keeping the consequences for members visible.
